Mylapore to Nowhere

# Mylapore to Nowhere

### How a Mylapore Girl Traded Ragas for Release Cycles, Saw the World, and Accidentally Entered into a Live-in Relationship with Her Laptop

[](https://substack.com/@amaruvi)

![Amaruvi Devanathan's avatar](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Bq_i!,w_36,h_36,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F357700fd-8e69-44fa-a5f8-000e6e26808a_1002x1002.jpeg)

“Sir, this is not an interview.”

Anita Subramaniam stirred her second filter coffee.

“This is a complaint.”

“A complaint?”

“No.”

She thought for a moment.

“A bug report.”

That seemed more appropriate.

After all, Anita was a Technical Architect in one of Chennai’s largest IT firms. Human emotions apparently had to be expressed in software terminology.

We were seated at Saravana Bhavan, the slowly self-destructing restaurant that lives on its past glory. Outside, autos were conducting a constitutional challenge against traffic rules. Inside, retired uncles were discussing geopolitics with the confidence of men who had never once been consulted by any government.

I had recognized Anita immediately.

Not because she was famous.

But because she looked exactly like every successful Indian IT professional over thirty-five.

Expensive phone.

Corporate backpack.

Intelligent eyes.

Permanent exhaustion.

The face of a woman who had attended three meetings before breakfast.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

She had approached me after a literary event.

“Sir, I have read your *Neyveli Kathaikal*.”

That got my attention.

Then she added:

“And *Vandhavarkal*.”

That got her a chair. A young female reader having read two of my books is as rare as a TVK MLA who knew why he got elected.

Most people mention YouTube.

Readers mention books.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“Actually,” she said, “I first saw your viral video.”

“Which one?”

“The one about old Brahmin parents sitting alone in Mylapore while their children enjoy life in America.”

“Ah.”

That video.

The one that had unexpectedly travelled farther than I ever had.

Thousands had watched it.

Hundreds wrote to me.

Several cried.

Apparently loneliness has excellent market penetration.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“My parents watched it.”

“Oh?”

“They cried.”

I nodded.

Many had.

“Then I cried.”

“Why?”

She smiled sadly.

“Because I realized one day I am going to become those parents.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

That was how the evening began.

And once Anita started talking, years of accumulated frustration poured out like the Cooum during a cyclone.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Life I Was Supposed To Have

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

“Sir, do you know what I was originally supposed to become?”

“No.”

“A proper Mylapore girl.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Now that statement requires explanation.

To outsiders, a “proper Mylapore girl” may sound like a location-specific human resource category.

To Tamilians, it means something very precise.

Carnatic music.

Bharatanatyam.

Filter coffee.

Temple visits.

December season concerts.

Respectable academic performance.

Strong opinions about semiya upma and why samba rava upma is never samba nor rava, leave alone upma.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“My grandmother had everything planned.”

“Of course.”

“I was supposed to learn music.”

“Naturally.”

“I was supposed to perform an arangetram.”

“Mandatory.”

“I was supposed to marry a decent boy.”

“Reasonable.”

“I was supposed to spend December arguing about concerts.”

“A noble ambition.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Instead she became a software engineer.

The Y2K bug destroyed more traditional Indian life plans than any social revolution.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“One day my mother was proudly telling people I knew Kalyani and Bhairavi.”

“The ragas.”

“Correct.”

“The next day she was proudly telling people I knew C++ and Java.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The veena went upstairs into storage.

The laptop came downstairs.

Globalization had arrived.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Great Middle-Class Upgrade

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Like thousands of middle-class Tamil girls, Anita entered the software industry at exactly the right time.

The dream years of the 2000s.

The magical years.

The years when every family believed software engineering was a government-approved shortcut to prosperity.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“Sir, we genuinely thought we were changing history.”

“You were.”

“We thought we had escaped.”

“Escaped what?”

She laughed.

“Everything.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The answer was not entirely wrong.

Women of Anita’s generation gained something extraordinary.

Financial independence.

Mobility.

Choice.

Agency.

Freedom.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“My grandmother needed permission.”

“My mother needed approval.”

“And you?”

“I needed a laptop.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Yet every revolution carries hidden invoices.

The bill simply arrives later.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Japan, Singapore and Other Forms of Loneliness

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

“People think overseas assignments are glamorous.”

“They can be.”

“They can also be lonely enough to qualify as a medical condition.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Her first assignment was Japan.

The second was Singapore.

Then another Singapore assignment followed by frequent USA sojourns.

Then a regional role.

Then a leadership role.

Then promotions.

Then more travel.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“I have seen Tokyo.”

“Beautiful city.”

“I have seen Singapore.”

“Beautiful city.”

“Been in and worked my heart out in California.”

“No wonder.”

“I have seen airports.”

“Every IT professional’s natural habitat.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

She laughed.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“The funny thing is, wherever I went, I kept searching for Mylapore.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

In Tokyo she searched for temple bells.

In Singapore she searched for the smell of fresh jasmine.

In California and Dallas she searched for Adai Aviyal and Kapalesswara.

In hotel rooms she searched for familiarity.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“You know what is funny?”

“What?”

“I travelled the world only to discover I missed vegetable vendors.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The soul is stubborn.

It doesn’t always want what LinkedIn wants.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Colorado, Trump and Modern Marriage

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

At some point her phone buzzed.

She glanced at it.

Not husband.

Not daughter.

Not parent.

Outlook.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“Sir, I think I am in a live-in relationship with my computer.”

That got my attention.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“No, seriously.”

She leaned forward.

“I spend more time with it than with my husband.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Her husband Subra worked for another software company.

Currently he was in Colorado.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“I probably shouldn’t be discussing these things with another man.”

“Correct.”

“My husband would agree.”

“Excellent.”

“But my husband is currently in Colorado.”

“Ah.”

“Addressing a server outage in Trump-infested America.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

I nearly dropped my coffee.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“The server appears to be receiving more attention than I do.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

This, unfortunately, is how many modern IT marriages operate.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

She and Subra share a home.

A mortgage.

A child.

Health insurance.

Mutual funds.

Netflix subscriptions.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

What they do not consistently share is geography.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“When I’m in Chennai, he is abroad.”

“When he returns?”

“I get sent somewhere.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The marriage survives.

But mostly through video calls and logistics management.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“Romance has become operational governance.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Ticket Number: Marriage

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

“We communicate exactly like project managers.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

She opened WhatsApp.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Milk subscription renewed?

School fee paid?

Gas cylinder booked?

Electricity bill cleared?

Parent-teacher meeting tomorrow.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

No poetry.

No mystery.

No excitement.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Just infrastructure maintenance.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“Sir, sometimes I think Subra and I are co-founders of a startup called Family Pvt Ltd.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The startup is functioning.

The founders are exhausted.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Samykuktha

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Then we came to the difficult subject.

Her daughter.

Samyuktha.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Every parent has a different voice when speaking about their child.

Anita’s voice softened instantly.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“That’s where the guilt lives.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Not in her job.

Not in her marriage.

Not in her ambitions.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

In motherhood.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“Do you know what Samyuktha asked me recently?”

“What?”

“Are you staying or visiting?”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The question landed heavily.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Anita had just returned from a lengthy overseas assignment.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“When your own child asks whether you are staying or visiting, you start questioning your life choices.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Children don’t accuse.

They observe.

That makes it worse.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“She has become very independent.”

“Good.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because she became independent before she needed to.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

That sentence lingered. And her eyes moistened.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Childhood We Outsourced

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Samyuktha belongs to a generation raised by multiple stakeholders.

Parents.

Teachers.

Daycare centres.

iPads.

Algorithms.

YouTube.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“My daughter knows American nursery rhymes.”

“Normal.”

“She knows Minecraft.”

“Expected.”

“She knows how to operate an iPad better than my mother.”

“Impressive.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

A pause. A distant look at the softly rotating ceiling fan.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“But she doesn’t know half the stories my grandmother told me.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The tragedy wasn’t dramatic.

It was incremental.

Tiny losses.

Tiny absences.

Tiny disconnects.

Accumulating quietly.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Diseases of Success

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

At some point Anita laughed.

A long, knowing laugh.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“Sir, my grandmother collected devotional songs.”

“Yes.”

“I collect medical reports.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The scorecard was impressive.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Thyroid issues.

Vitamin D deficiency.

Borderline diabetes.

Stress-induced gastritis.

Insomnia.

Anxiety.

Cervical spondylosis.

Early hypertension.

PCOS.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“IT has produced many unicorns.”

“True.”

“It has also produced an impressive collection of endocrinology patients.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Nobody tells young graduates this.

The body keeps score.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

At forty-two, Anita knew every specialist in Chennai.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Cardiologist.

Orthopaedic doctor.

Endocrinologist.

Physiotherapist.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“Sometimes I think my medical team has more visibility into my life than my relatives.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Mylapore Fantasy

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Eventually I asked the obvious question.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“If you could redesign your life, what would it look like?”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

She smiled.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“A boring life.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“Boring?”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“Very boring.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

She sat back.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“I would wake up.”

“Okay.”

“Make coffee.”

“Good.”

“Go to temple.”

“Fine.”

“Attend a concert.”

“Reasonable.”

“Teach Samyuktha a few songs.”

“Excellent.”

“Spend time with Subra.”

“Revolutionary.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

I laughed.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

She wasn’t joking.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The fantasy wasn’t wealth.

The fantasy wasn’t luxury.

The fantasy wasn’t Europe.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The fantasy was time.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## But Mylapore Isn’t Mylapore Anymore

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Then she surprised me.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“Actually, I don’t even want the old Mylapore.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“No?”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“It doesn’t exist.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

She wasn’t wrong.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The old Mylapore survives mostly in memory.

The sabhas remain.

The temples remain.

The coffee remains.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

But the city itself has changed.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Children leave.

Parents age.

Apartments replace houses.

WhatsApp replaces conversations.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The loneliness simply wears better clothes now.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Question Nobody Answers

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The evening was ending.

Saravana Bhavan was, kind of, emptying.

Mylapore was preparing for another night of traffic, noise and nostalgia.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Anita looked outside.

Then at me.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“Sir.”

“Yes.”

“Do you think we made a mistake?”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

A dangerous question.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

I considered it carefully.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“No.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

She seemed surprised.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“No?”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“No.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Her generation achieved remarkable things.

They transformed Indian society.

They expanded opportunities.

They broke barriers.

They created possibilities their mothers never had.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The problem wasn’t success.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The problem was assuming success would automatically create happiness.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Those are different projects.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

And they have different delivery timelines.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Anita smiled. A tired smile. But a genuine one.

“You know what , Sir ? I sometimes think, the ‘Janaki’ character in your ‘Vandhavarkal’ novel, she is still alive. And it is me. Probably should’ve been me in my previous birth”

For a moment I was stunned. Janaki was the central character in my period novel ‘Vandhavarkal’. But she spent most of her time as a widow.

I squeezed my eyebrows and looked quizzically.

“Yes Sir. I know what is running in your mind. There is no difference between me and her. We both are waiting to join our husbands. Hers was a traditional database. Mine is the realtime Kafka-Couchbase-Mongo system. Don’t you think so?”

My heart was shaken and I kept mum for a while. Too much to put Anita in my Janaki character’s place.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

As we got up to leave, she said something I have not forgotten.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“Maybe that is what I miss.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“What?”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“The feeling.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“What feeling?”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

She looked toward the distant lights of Kapaleeswarar Temple.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“The feeling that life was something to be lived.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

A pause.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“Not continuously delivered.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

“And for a few moments, just to hold Subra’s hands while resting my cheek on his shoulder, with Samyuktha trying to pull down his glasses. This has not happened for a long long time.”

And a long pause, a clumsy ‘Namaste’ sign followed by a quick exit with teary eyes.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

And there, perhaps, lies the story of an entire generation.

A generation that exchanged jasmine flowers for access cards.

Veenas for laptops.

Sabhas for conference rooms.

Ragas for release cycles.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

A generation that conquered the world.

Travelled everywhere.

Earned everything.

Bought homes.

Raised children.

Built careers.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

And then occasionally found itself sitting in a restaurant in Mylapore, talking to a writer about old parents, missing husbands, distant children, forgotten music lessons, and the strange realization that the most expensive thing they had ever lost was not money.

It was time.
